prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B046 prize for Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The tally is not my reason. The science is complete and independently confirmed over decades, running from the physiology of GLP-1 secretion and incretin action (Holst), through proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology and the path to therapy (Drucker), to long-acting analogues with randomized outcome data in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease (Knudsen). For a Physiology or Medicine prize, the physiology and the medicine it produced are one achievement, and a citation that names both is accurate. A single part keeps the three-person cap workable and avoids diluting the strongest case with a weaker second part.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still credit. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide is a real contribution that my trio leaves out, and the Habener group is outside the supplied names altogether. Putting an industrial developer in the third place invites the criticism that we reward drug development over discovery. Nobody in round 1, including me, has verified the priority record from the supplied evidence, so I am choosing between two imperfect trios under uncertainty. Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy for obesity are also still accumulating, though I do not consider that a barrier to recognition now.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and says he would move toward the Knudsen trio if Mojsov's work cannot be separated from the Habener group or verified.
responses.response: In round 1 I said I would accept a swap if B046 were framed as a discovery prize. Your own condition is the point that settles it for me. The supplied record does not let us separate Mojsov's contribution from the Habener group's, and a citation naming a contested priority claim while leaving out the same group is harder to defend than one resting on documented physiology and documented development. Your trio also leaves out the person whose analogues are the medicine, so a citation that mentions incretin treatment would stop short of what it cites. I therefore keep Knudsen. If someone shows that Mojsov's work was independent and necessary, I would reopen this and move toward your trio.

responses.point: Argues that the three places should cover the discovery side (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov), and that omitting Knudsen risks a prize that stops short of the clinical achievement it cites.
responses.response: I agree with your closing worry and see it as the argument for Knudsen. You say that without her the prize risks stopping short of the clinical achievement. You also say Mojsov carries attribution risk. Those two points together favour my configuration. Where we differ is on weighting. You read the statutes as pointing to discovery; I read the remit as covering physiology that reaches patients, and the Drucker-Holst-Knudsen arc is a clean example. I accept that this is a judgment of weighting and not a factual disagreement. I also note that your CAR-T concern about Eshhar stands, which is why I would not add B037 as a second part.

responses.point: Supports the Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio but says that if the committee judges the Mojsov claim decisive, that configuration is the weaker reading. He also notes that adding B014 would make four laureates against the cap.
responses.response: I share that caveat and want it in the public record: the conditional you describe is the real risk to my position. What persuades me to hold is that no member has shown the Mojsov claim to be decisive and separable, and every member who addresses it calls it unverified. Your arithmetic on a second part is also right. B014 would add Walter and Mori to a trio that already uses the cap, and I do not think B014 or any other part is strong enough to justify dropping one of the B046 names. B014 has the cleaner attribution, but the benefit to patients is still largely prospective, so I keep it as an alternative and not as a second part.

responses.point: Raises, as chair, whether a citation can be worded to make the exclusion of Mojsov, the Habener group and the fourth credited name explicit and principled, and whether the committee can defend either omission.
responses.response: I do not think a citation can make the omission principled by wording alone, and I would not try to hide it. The best we can do is to define the achievement in the citation as the physiology of GLP-1 and its development into therapy, which is what my text does, and let the credited names follow from that definition. I would not add a clause that adjudicates priority between Mojsov and the Habener group, because the supplied evidence does not allow it. The omission of Mojsov is a cost I accept knowingly. On your question about a second part, I see no clear gain, and I agree with Linnarsson that B046 stands best alone.

responses.point: Also prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, and describes a single achievement credited with both the discovery and the translation as what the history requires.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration, but I will not treat that as confirmation, since we both rest on the same unverified priority record. My reasoning differs slightly from yours. You rely on the translational argument as the justification, while I think the physiology half also stands on Drucker and Holst alone, so the case does not depend on Knudsen being decisive. That matters if the committee later adds Mojsov in her place: the discovery-to-therapy arc would remain defensible, though the citation would then need to be narrowed to avoid claiming the analogues.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide was independent and necessary relative to the Habener group; I have not verified this and neither has any other member.
Whether the committee will accept a discovery-to-therapy citation for B046 or insist on a discovery-only framing, which would change the third name.
Whether CAR-T (B037) can be credited defensibly when Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept lies outside the supplied names, which matters only if B046 stalls.
Whether the long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy for obesity will change how the achievement is regarded; I judge it not to be a barrier now.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal issue has emerged for B046, B037 or B014 in the round-1 exchange, and none of the chair's flags involves a shortlisted candidate or credited name. My profile lists a 2009 co-authored paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, which does not concern the candidates I propose, and I note for transparency that Perlmann prefers a different third laureate for B046. My motor-circuit field is adjacent to optogenetics (B030), which I do not propose. No disclosure has changed since round 1.
